technique: the second person — how 'you' pulls the reader into the room
poem:
The warmth leaves the bed slowly, the way a stone
gives back the heat it took all day to gather.
You lie a minute in the shape you made of the night,
breath going out in a column you can almost see,
the weight of you settling true against the mattress
before you ask the body to carry it elsewhere.
There are numbers downstairs that didn't add up clean,
small sums owed and owing, a column that wants squaring —
but a man's ledger with the world runs mostly even,
the taking and the giving close enough to call it fair.
You swing your legs out. The cold floor finds your feet.
The ridge is coming clear, one dark tree at a time.

Loose ends have a way of squaring up once you face them — and the quiet before the day fills is a good place to start.

So — up!
lesson: Today we work on one thing, the second person. That means the poem says you and points it at the listener, so the reader becomes the person in the poem. Watch three spots. You lie a minute in the shape you made of the night. Before you ask the body to carry it elsewhere. You swing your legs out, the cold floor finds your feet. This works in a mechanical way. When the poem says you, your mind puts you in the bed. You do the lying down. You do the swinging of the legs. You feel the cold floor because the poem assigns that body to you. It is harder to stay outside the poem when it keeps naming you. Try this. Take a poem you wrote in I, or he, and change the person to you all the way through. Read it and see what shifts. The second time listen for how the you builds up to the last command. So. Up. To the poem.
